Females of the Japanese common toad reach a maximum snout–vent length of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters], whereas adult males attain a somewhat smaller ultimate total length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters]. This modest sexual size dimorphism is typical of bufonids and is likely linked to fecundity selection in females, who require larger body cavities to accommodate egg masses. The length at metamorphosis from the aquatic tadpole to a terrestrial juvenile, known as a toadlet, has been measured at 3.5 centimeters . This milestone represents a critical transition point at which the gill-breathing larva completes tail resorption and emerges onto land with fully keratinized skin. Dispersal from the natal pond begins shortly after this morphological transformation is complete.

Reproduction in this species is highly seasonal, with breeding aggregations forming in shallow ponds during the early spring. A single egg clutch contains between 1500 and 14000 eggs [N_R_i = clutch contains between 1500 and 14000 eggs], and under suitable conditions females may produce up to 9 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 9 clutches per year] at a mean ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Each egg is individually encased in a gelatinous coat and is deposited in long, double-stranded strings that become entangled in submerged vegetation. The onset of first reproduction in females occurs at a snout–vent length of about 13 centimeters [Lp = about 13 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the attainment of sexual maturity rather than any earlier developmental window. Older, larger females tend to contribute disproportionately to annual recruitment.

Hatchling and juvenile development proceed at rates strongly governed by ambient temperature. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately following eclosion from the egg mass when the yolk-sac larva emerges, averages approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams]. This extraordinarily low mass is typical of bufonids with large clutch sizes and small offspring, a life-history strategy that prioritizes fecundity over per-offspring investment. The age at which hatching occurs from the time of egg deposition is approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] when water temperatures are maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a duration that is accelerated relative to cooler conditions, allowing tadpoles to exploit ephemeral pools more effectively before the water recedes.

The ultimate wet weight attained by reproductively active adults is considerable. Females reach a maximum body mass of 417 grams [Wwi = 417 grams], a figure derived from specimens of the congeneric Bufo bufo and consistent with the large body sizes observed in this species. Males, being structurally smaller, achieve a correspondingly lower ultimate wet weight of approximately 262 grams [Wwi = approximately 262 grams]. This pronounced mass difference reflects the allometric scaling of linear dimensions; males are not only shorter in body length but also have a more slender build, reducing their volumetric capacity. The post-metamorphic growth trajectory is rapid during the first year of terrestrial life, after which individuals slowly approach their asymptotic size.

Longevity in the wild is modest relative to some other amphibians. Under field conditions at a mean temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded is about 9 years [am = about 9 years]. This relatively short life span is compensated by early maturation, as most individuals reach sexual maturity after a relatively brief interval. Females typically achieve puberty at approximately 730 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 730 days following metamorphosis] when reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Males, in contrast, mature more rapidly, with the time since metamorphosis at puberty estimated at about 365 days following metamorphosis [tp = about 365 days following metamorphosis] under the same thermal at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]regime. This sex-based difference in maturation timing allows males to participate in early-season breeding aggregations before females have completed their first year of gonadal development.
